title: Depression: recognising symptoms and finding a workable treatment plan
intro: Depression can affect mood, interest, energy, sleep, thinking and physical health. It is a treatable illness, not a test of character or gratitude. Some people mainly feel sad; others feel numb, irritable or unable to manage ordinary tasks. Support should take both symptoms and real difficulties such as isolation, discrimination, money worries or illness seriously.

sections.heading: Recognise a persistent change
paragraphs: Low mood or loss of interest most days for roughly two weeks is a reason to seek assessment, especially with sleep or appetite changes, fatigue, poor concentration, guilt or hopelessness. Do not wait for that duration if distress is severe or safety is at risk. Depression can occur after a loss or without an obvious event, and it may coexist with grief, anxiety or physical illness. Children may show irritability rather than sadness and need age-appropriate assessment. A screening score can start a conversation but does not establish the diagnosis by itself.

sections.heading: A useful assessment looks beyond a label
paragraphs: Tell the clinician when symptoms started, how daily life is affected, previous episodes, medicines, alcohol or drug use and available support. Mention periods of unusually high or irritable mood, little need for sleep, racing thoughts or impulsive behaviour: these can suggest bipolar illness and change treatment. Medical conditions such as thyroid disease and medicine effects may resemble or worsen depression. Tests are used when appropriate to investigate these, rather than as a single blood test for depression. Ask for an interpreter or another way to explain symptoms if language or literacy makes the discussion difficult.

sections.heading: Choose treatment together and review progress
paragraphs: Options include guided self-help, psychological therapies such as behavioural activation, cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy, and antidepressant medication when suitable. Choice depends on severity, previous response, preference, access and other health conditions. A combination may be helpful, particularly for more severe illness. Agree practical goals and a review date rather than leaving the person to wait indefinitely. If the first approach does not help, reassess diagnosis, barriers, tolerability and other options; lack of improvement is not personal failure. Severe or persistent depression may need specialist treatments, and sometimes hospital care.

sections.heading: Medicines need a follow-up and stopping plan
paragraphs: Antidepressants take time to work and can cause side effects before benefits are clear. Discuss sleep, digestive or sexual effects and interactions, including herbal products such as St John's wort. Arrange early review after starting or changing treatment. New agitation, suicidal thoughts or marked mood elevation need prompt medical advice; immediate danger needs emergency care. Younger people require particular monitoring. Do not stop abruptly when feeling better or because of side effects: withdrawal can be difficult, and a clinician should help plan gradual changes. Pregnancy or breastfeeding also needs an individual benefit-and-risk discussion rather than automatic discontinuation.

sections.heading: Practical support and safety are part of care
paragraphs: Small achievable steps, regular meals, a manageable sleep routine, suitable activity and contact with trusted people can support treatment. They are not demands to cure yourself through willpower. Family or friends can help book an appointment, provide transport or share tasks with permission. If thoughts of self-harm or suicide arise, tell a healthcare professional promptly and seek support from someone trusted. If you may act on them, cannot stay safe, have already harmed yourself, or have severe confusion or distressing psychotic symptoms, seek emergency help now. Ask someone to stay with you while help is arranged. Agree a safety and relapse plan with the treating team, including whom to contact if symptoms worsen.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: help with the first step
examples.text: For several weeks, Arben has stopped meeting friends and struggles to prepare meals. His sister listens without telling him to be more positive. With his agreement she helps arrange an appointment and accompanies him, while he describes his own symptoms and goals.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: reviewing rather than abandoning treatment
examples.text: Mira begins treatment but develops troublesome nausea and still feels low. She contacts the prescriber, who checks safety, timing and side effects and agrees the next steps. She does not suddenly stop the medicine or conclude that no treatment can ever help.

questions: Could another illness, medicine or bipolar symptoms affect this assessment?
Which treatment fits my needs, and when will we review its effects?
What is my plan for worsening symptoms, side effects or a safety crisis?
